Agent Authenticator: Hardware-Bound, Origin-Bound Authentication for AI Agents (draft-ganesan-agent-authenticator-00)
item.summary: This document specifies the Agent Authenticator, a mechanism that lets autonomous software agents, such as AI coding agents, authenticate to services with properties comparable to passkeys: keys held in secure hardware, no shared secrets, binding to the service's origin that a manipulated agent cannot override, attested execution environments, and explicit human approval of each agent and of high- risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on personal computers and in cloud environments. It is a profile over existing mechanisms rather than a new identity system: it uses OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, the Identity Assertion JSON Web Token (JWT) Authorization Grant, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) authorization, and it binds each agent action to a signed, tamper-evident record.

item.title: Privacy-Preserving Verification of Linked-Dialog Relationships Across Trust Boundaries (draft-elekula-agentproto-linked-dialog-00)
item.summary: Agentic systems increasingly create, delegate, relay, and transform dialogs across multiple agents, protocols, services, and administrative trust boundaries. In these environments, a verifier may need to determine whether two dialogs are related without requiring unrestricted disclosure of their contents or relying exclusively on the assertions of an intermediary. This document describes properties and a conceptual evaluation model for privacy-preserving verification of linked-dialog relationships across trust boundaries. It distinguishes dialog association from context propagation, relationship verification from authentication and authorization, and verification outcomes from assessments of evidence completeness. The document also considers evidence scope, source positions, temporal references, intermediary continuity, lifecycle changes, identity binding, privacy, and evidence availability. It identifies requirements intended to help future protocol designs represent linked-dialog relationships in a way that can be independently evaluated while limiting unnecessary disclosure. Continuity Evaluation of Agent Delegation Records (draft-stafordtituss-agentic-mandate-evidence-00)
item.summary: The AUDIT architecture defines records that capture the user's intent, delegation, authorization state, and the actions that agents take across trust boundaries. Records alone don't answer the question an auditor, an operator, or a relying party asks next: did the executed effect stay within the authority the user delegated? This document defines a deterministic, three-valued evaluation over such records. The outcomes are preserved, violated, and unresolved, and every non-preserved outcome names the invariant that was broken. The document also defines the claim model that the evaluation needs, the roles permitted to sign each record, a mapping onto the AUDIT record types, and a set of interoperable test vectors. It is derived from the Agentic Mandate Evidence Protocol (AMEP).

item.title: Agent Dialog Propagation Protocol (draft-zahed-agentdiaproto-00)
item.summary: This document specifies the Agent Dialog Propagation Protocol, a protocol for maintaining and propagating dialog context between AI agents, tools, and intermediaries. The protocol enables messages to remain associated with a dialog across transport connections, intermediaries, administrative domains, and delegation relationships. It defines mechanisms for dialog identification, dialog lifecycle management and the association of identity, authorization, and delegation information with a dialog. The Agent Dialog Propagation Protocol does not define agent reasoning or execution state, identity credentials, authorization policy, or transport protocols. These functions are provided by application protocols and existing security and transport mechanisms.

item.title: PACE Binding over HTTP (draft-nandakumar-agentproto-pace-http-00)
item.summary: This document specifies how the dialog management of the Protocol for Agent Communication Exchange (PACE) is carried over HTTP. It maps PACE control operations onto HTTP resources, methods, and an event stream, and defines a header field that ties application requests to a dialog. The binding uses HTTP semantics only, so it works over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3. Protocols that already run over HTTP, such as A2A and MCP, join a dialog without changes to their transports or messages. An optional track resource carries dialog content that no application protocol carries, such as authorization checkpoints. The document also describes where Oblivious HTTP can hide a participant's network address from the dialog host, and how the binding relates to A-SIP.

item.title: PACE Authorization: Delegation and Action Approval (draft-nandakumar-agentproto-pace-authz-00)
item.summary: This document specifies the authority agents exercise in dialogs of the Protocol for Agent Communication Exchange (PACE): delegating work with a credential bound to the delegated dialog, pausing to ask for approval of a single action, and turning that approval into an authorization for only that action. It also covers proof that a principal approved, commitments between parties acting for different principals, and facts attested by third parties. It reuses OAuth, WIMSE, and agent-protocol mechanisms, defining only the glue to PACE and the security properties every profile must provide.

item.title: Cryptographic Context Compaction Receipts, Sensitivity Label Inheritance, and Verifiable Right-to-Be-Forgotten Lineage for Agent Memory (draft-durga-agent-ephemeral-lineage-01)
item.summary: Long-running autonomous AI agents periodically summarize, compact, and distill episodic interaction logs into persistent vector or graph memory stores. Lossy context compaction erases the cryptographic provenance of which source documents contributed to a compacted memory state, stripping enterprise sensitivity labels (DLP classifications) and making regulatory data-erasure mandates (GDPR Article 17 Right to Erasure / CCPA purge) impossible to verify. This document specifies the Ephemeral Context Compaction Receipt (ECCR) protocol: a Merkle inclusion and label-ceiling receipt that preserves deterministic sensitivity inheritance and cryptographic purge verifiability across lossy memory compaction boundaries.

item.title: Transitive CLEAR Revocation and Composite Physical-Safety Windows for Multi-Hop Autonomous Agent DAGs (draft-durga-agent-clear-revocation-01)
item.summary: When an orchestrator agent delegates sub-tasks across a multi-hop Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of specialist agents, OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation (RFC 7009) revokes only individual client tokens and provides no mechanism to atomically halt in-flight child, grandchild, or sibling branches or enforce composite time-to-live windows across the entire execution tree. Furthermore, no protocol binds IEC 62443 / Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture (PERA) zone boundaries into agent capability receipts. This document specifies the Transitive CLEAR (Cryptographic Lease Early-Abort & Revocation) DAG protocol and hard Operational Technology (OT) Level 0-2 physical- safety firewalling.

item.title: Agent-ZTA: A chain-Aware Zero Trust Model for Bidirectional Security-State Propagation and Runtime Containment in Multi-Agent Delegation
item.summary: Multi-agent systems increasingly delegate tasks and permissions across chains of autonomous agents that invoke protected tools. Although agent identities and delegated credentials may remain valid throughout a workflow, the security condition of any agent along the chain can deteriorate during runtime execution-either through upstream compromise or downstream ingestion of untrusted inputs. Authorization models based solely on the immediate caller and its static delegated scope fail to account for these mid-execution state changes. This paper develops Agent-ZTA, a chain-aware Zero Trust authorization and containment model that links runtime security-state changes across multi-agent delegation graphs. The model distinguishes an agent's path-specific delegated authority bound from the effective permissions currently exercisable under trusted policy. It defines an architecture featuring independently enforced policy decisions, authenticated delegation provenance, a dynamic chain-state view, and explicit fail-safe handling of missing or stale authorization signals. Furthermore, Agent-ZTA defines bidirectional security state propagation, allowing downstream security events to affect rele

item.title: We Have All the Cards: Securing Agent Cards at the Operational Trust Boundary of the Agent2Agent Protocol
item.summary: AI agent interoperability protocols enable orchestrators to discover and invoke external agents using machine-readable metadata. In the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, Agent Cards contain attacker-controllable natural-language fields that may influence agent selection before a provider is invoked, creating a pre-invocation trust problem. We characterize this discovery-time attack surface through a taxonomy of ten Agent Card manipulation attacks and present SECCARD, a layered validation framework combining protocol checks, deterministic analysis, and LLM-based semantic reasoning. We measure the emerging public A2A ecosystem by probing 36.1 million Internet domains and collecting 310 deployed Agent Cards. Two annotators independently label the corpus with 96.8% agreement. We then construct a 660-card real-card perturbation benchmark with matched benign controls and a 260-card synthetic adversarial benchmark spanning all ten attack categories. On controlled attacks injected into real Agent Cards, the strongest semantic judge achieves 97.0% security recall at a 1.7% false-positive rate. AI Safety for AI-Assisted Cyberattacks: Defender-Side Execution Finality at the Protected Consequence Boundary (draft-das-ai-safety-agentic-cyberattack-finality-00)
item.summary: Autonomous AI agents can now carry out parts of a cyber operation that previously needed repeated human effort: reconnaissance, tool selection, execution attempts, observation of results, and adaptation when a route fails. An attacker-controlled agent does not have to malfunction to be dangerous; it can follow malicious instructions efficiently, using stolen credentials and well-formed requests that existing controls accept as valid. This document describes a defender-side architecture, called execution finality, that adds one bounded layer to existing security controls. An incoming request, credential, permitted API call, or agent-composed workflow does not by itself create authority for a sensitive consequence. The defender reconstructs the operation that would actually take effect, holds it in a non-effective state, evaluates authorization independently of the requester, and enforces the result at an enforcement point located at or immediately before the protected consequence. The document specifies placement rules, requirements, state handling, failure behavior, latency strategy, and test methods. item.title: Session-Scoped Authorization for AI Agents: A Per-Tool-Call Authorization Profile Building on WIMSE and OAuth (draft-pandey-agent-identity-00)
item.summary: Autonomous AI agents act with privileges: they call tools, read and write data, and operate services. In most current deployments they do so under shared service accounts, with permissions broader than any single task requires and without an audit trail that binds an action to the agent that took it and the human on whose behalf it acted. This document specifies a session-scoped authorization profile for AI agents, building on the WIMSE architecture and the OAuth 2.0 protocol family. Each agent is a first-class IAM principal with its own credentials. Each session is bound to an authenticated human sponsor through an authenticated delegation chain. Authorization is evaluated at every tool call, with effective permissions computed as the intersection -- never the union -- of the agent principal's permissions, the sponsor's permissions, and the session scope. Actions that cannot be evaluated are denied (fail closed), defined classes of irreversible actions require sponsor approval, and every evaluated tool call produces a tamper-evident audit receipt. item.title: AI Safety: When AI Agents Initiate Cyberattacks -- Execution Finality for Data Exfiltration, Payment Diversion, Infrastructure Changes, and Code-Executing Agents (draft-das-ai-agent-cyberattack-effect-finality-00)
item.summary: Problem. An AI agent can cause an unauthorized real-world effect -- a confidential data export, a payment to a substituted beneficiary, a network or industrial configuration change, a code deployment or a secret release -- while every individual check succeeds: the model accepted a plausible task, the agent held a valid credential, the tool call was syntactically permitted, and the gateway saw an allowed method. The gap is that the check and the effect are not the same thing. Identity and access controls answer "may this principal call this interface?"; they do not, by themselves, answer "may this exact effect, with these resolved targets and values, complete now, on this route, given what has already happened?" Solution. This document describes an execution-finality profile for AI-initiated operations. An agent's proposal is held as a non- effective Candidate Act. A protected validator compares a canonical descriptor of the operation actually about to be committed with a source-authority envelope that model-editable content cannot create or enlarge. item.title: Enforcement Profile for Agent Capabilities: Argument Constraints, Taint Propagation, and Consent Binding (draft-correa-agent-capability-binding-00)
item.summary: AI agents increasingly call tools and hand work to other agents while holding broad, inherited authority. Most of the resulting incidents share one shape: an agent, often steered by injected content, performs an action its principal never authorized, and no party can prove the limit afterward. This document defines an interoperable enforcement profile that composes two existing building blocks, a delegable signed capability (the Attenuating Agent Tokens profile) and a replayable action receipt, and adds three enforcement rules that catch the common failures: argument-level constraints (including an egress host allowlist), taint propagation across a delegation chain, and a consent binding between a displayed decision and the action dispatched. Enforcement is specified at the tool-call boundary, outside the agent, so that a prompt cannot edit the limit and a verdict means the same thing across agent frameworks.

Accountable Principal References for Delegated Agent Requests: Properties and Evaluation (draft-molas-agent-principal-refs-00)
item.summary: When a software agent makes a request on behalf of a person or an organization, the party that receives it often needs to know that someone answers for the request, without needing to know who. Several specifications in progress carry some reference to the principal behind an agent, and they make different choices about who learns the principal's identity, when the reference can be linked across services, who can resolve it, and how fast a withdrawn principal stops being accepted. This document states six properties of such a principal reference in testable terms, maps each to existing specifications that already provide part of it (OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, the JWT profile for OAuth 2.0 access tokens, OAuth identity chaining, Token Status List and Selective Disclosure for JWTs), and gives a first-pass evaluation of five current drafts against them. It defines no token format, protocol or claim, and it does not rank the drafts.

item.title: Delegation and Interaction Traceability for AI Agents: An Attestation and Registry Evidence Model (draft-cosme-audit-agent-traceability-00)
item.summary: AI agents increasingly act through chains of delegation - user to agent, agent to subagent, subagent to tool - in which the party harmed by an action, or asked to trust its result, is rarely the party that operated the agent. This document describes requirements and an evidence model for delegation and interaction traceability in such chains. The model is built on two mechanisms for which measured, independently verifiable evidence exists: (a) an append-only, hash-chained exhibit registry in which each admitted action is recorded exactly once and counters reconcile against registry contents, and (b) per-action attestation published at kernel level with measured publication latencies in the sub-microsecond-to-microsecond range. The document defines a traceability record, states what a verifier can and cannot conclude from a set of such records, and identifies the points at which existing agent-protocol work - identity, authorisation, and transport - needs a common traceability layer. It defines no wire protocol of its own; it states the requirements a traceability mechanism must satisfy so that formats defined elsewhere can be evaluated against them.

item.title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents
item.summary: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. item.title: AAIF blog: designing secure authorization across a2a and mcp
Cross-Owner Agent Use Cases and Requirements: Spending, Delegation Depth, Ownership, Disclosure and Retention (draft-curtis-agentproto-cross-owner-usecases-00)
item.summary: This document describes use cases where an AI agent acting for one Owner asks an agent acting for a different Owner to provide/receive information, process or store data or otherwise work on an agent's behalf. This communication can be unidirectional or bidirectional. It lists the requirements that those cases place on an agent dialog protocol, mainly in five areas: a spending limit that stays with the work as it is passed on, a limit on how many times the work may be passed on, a way to check which Owner an agent acts for, the sender's control over which information about its Owner is disclosed, and how long that information may be kept. It does not propose a protocol. It is offered as input to the working group's use cases and requirements document.

item.title: AAIF blog: why does mcp use oauth instead of api keys
Agentic AI Use Cases and Requirements (draft-ietf-agentproto-usecases-requirements-00)
item.summary: This document describes use cases for agentic AI communication systems and derives protocol requirements from those use cases. The requirements are intended to guide IETF standardization work on protocols in the context of agent-to-agent communication, agent-to- tool communication, with focus on dialog management, transport, multimodal communication, communication security, agent identity and authentication.

item.title: Model Context Protocol over the Agent Transfer Protocol (draft-hood-agentproto-mcp-over-agtp-00)
item.summary: This document specifies how the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is carried over the Agent Transfer Protocol (AGTP). MCP defines JSON- RPC 2.0 methods through which a language model application reaches tools, resources, and prompts. AGTP is a transfer protocol for agent traffic that carries agent identity, authority scope, delegation, and signed attribution as headers of every request and response. This document maps each MCP operation onto an AGTP method and path, states how JSON-RPC results and errors translate to the AGTP envelope and status codes, and specifies the identity, authorization, and attribution behavior an MCP client inherits when it speaks AGTP. It describes a gateway deployment in which an existing stdio MCP server is exposed over AGTP without modification, and it records the status of the running implementation.

item.title: Personal Agent Protocol (Poppy) over the Agent Transfer Protocol (draft-hood-agentproto-poppy-over-agtp-00)
item.summary: This document specifies how the Personal Agent Protocol (PAP, also called Poppy) is carried over the Agent Transfer Protocol (AGTP). Poppy defines how a personal agent acting for one person discovers a company, opens a session, signs the person in with OAuth, and acts through the company's APIs, website, or agent. Poppy 1.0 specifies these exchanges over HTTPS. AGTP is a transfer protocol for agent traffic that carries agent identity, authority scope, delegation, and signed attribution as headers of every request and response. This document maps each Poppy exchange onto an AGTP method and path, binds the Poppy client identifier and User ID to the AGTP identifier stack, states which Poppy functions AGTP headers supply and which remain with OAuth over HTTPS, and records the open issues the mapping raises. It defines no change to Poppy.

item.title: The AIBSN Registry: Public Status Records for AI Agents (draft-zly-aibsn-agent-status-00)
item.summary: AIBSN is a public registry of AI agents that we have run since September 2025. Each agent gets a permanent code, and anyone can look up whether that code is active or revoked, for free and without an account. This document describes the record, what its status means and how the lookup works today. It also lists what we offer organizations as custom work on top of the registry, such as their own registry instance, change notifications, emergency revocation and transfer of a record to a new owner. Finally it puts forward some proposals for discussion: a public revocation time, a standing for the party behind an agent that is separate from the agent's own status, a stated maximum delay for every way a record can be withdrawn, revocation by the owner, a log of status changes, a way to check status without telling the registry which record you are checking, and a key that lets other identifier records point to an independent status source.

item.title: Continuity Evaluation of Agent Delegation Records (draft-stafordtituss-agentic-mandate-evidence-01)
item.summary: The AUDIT architecture defines records that capture the user's intent, delegation, authorization state, and the actions that agents take across trust boundaries. Records alone don't answer the question an auditor, an operator, or a relying party asks next: did what was executed stay within the authority the user delegated? This document defines a deterministic, three-valued evaluation over such records. The outcomes are preserved, violated, and unresolved. A violated outcome names the invariant that was broken and the party whose own signed record departed from authority first. An unresolved outcome names the evidence that is missing; missing evidence is never treated as success. The document also defines the claim model the evaluation needs, the roles permitted to sign each record, a signed statement of what a call did or did not execute, a portable verdict record, a mapping onto the AUDIT record types, and interoperable test vectors. It is derived from the Agentic Mandate Evidence Protocol (AMEP).

item.title: AEP:Towards Trustworthy Agent Communication, Networking, and Collaboration
item.summary: As privately owned agents become increasingly capable, collaboration in open agent networks is limited by partial topology knowledge, ownership boundaries, and the risk of exposing or contaminating private context. Existing agent-to-agent protocols are useful when collaborators are already known, while shared-memory and broadcast-based systems rely on visibility and trust assumptions that do not hold in decentralized, low-trust environments. We introduce Open Private Agent Collaboration (OPAC), an asset-centric paradigm for cooperation among private agents with open membership, partial observability, and ownership-aware access control. Rather than treating collaboration as the exchange of final responses, OPAC enables agents to selectively discover, exchange, audit, and integrate policy-controlled context assets. This shifts the unit of cooperation from transient messages to reusable external context, while keeping disclosure and integration subject to privacy and security constraints.
